slides.title: ChatGPT is about to sign its EU texts. *Invisibly.*
slides.subtitle: What it can prove, and what it can't.

slides.label: 01 · The news
slides.title: OpenAI announced it on 5 October.
slides.body: Over the coming weeks, eligible ChatGPT and Codex text made in the EU gets an invisible watermark. It's OpenAI's answer to the *EU AI Act*, which wants AI text to be machine-detectable.

slides.label: 02 · How it works
slides.title: It hides in word choice, not on screen.
slides.body: The method, called textGrain, nudges which words the model picks. A detector looks for that statistical pattern. Your text looks exactly the same.

slides.label: 03 · How reliable
slides.title: of 200-token passages detected.
slides.body: About 95% at 400 tokens, at a 1% false-positive target, for prose like psychology. Much lower for maths-like text, and editing weakens it. OpenAI says so itself.

left.label: Can't tell
items: That no watermark means a human wrote it

right.label: Can signal
items: That an OpenAI model made or processed part of it
Only if the passage is long enough

slides.label: 05 · Who can check
slides.title: Not your client. Not yet.
slides.body: The detector isn't public. At launch, only approved researchers and expert organisations can apply. In the API, watermarking is opt-in and *off by default*.

slides.title: What I'd do this week
items: Edit AI drafts for quality and facts, not to hide AI use.
Check client and creator contracts for AI-disclosure clauses.
Decide your own disclosure rule before a client asks.
Ignore 'AI detector' screenshots. They prove very little.
